$comment: Backup/restore POLICY as data (Task 047).
Three separate things live in this repository and this file holds the third:
deploy/backup/scope.json   WHAT is covered (tables, retention, restore order)
deploy/k8s/backup-cronjob.yaml  HOW it is produced (the job)
deploy/backup/policy.json  WHAT WE PROMISED (RPO/RTO, escalation, drill
cadence, the gap register, and the rule that makes
an open gap block a release)
scripts/check-backup-policy.mjs reads all three plus the migrations and fails
when they disagree. The required seven groups are written down a FOURTH time
in tools/backup-policy.test.mjs, which is the point: a check whose subject
list comes from the same file as the data it checks will always agree with
itself. That is not hypothetical - it is gaps D2, D6 and D7 in docs/backup.md.
RPO/RTO VALUES ARE TEAM-CHOSEN, NOT PLAN-DERIVED. Plan B section 18.4
specifies no RPO, no RTO, no job path and no escalation contact. Plan A
section 30 proposes RPO 5 min / RTO 1 h and those are the numbers carried
forward; what this file adds is which of them is a TARGET, which has been
MEASURED, and who to call. Replace every CHANGE_ME before this policy is
used to gate a real release.

coverage.$comment: The seven durable-entity groups. Id, title and table must match deploy/backup/scope.json and the CronJob's annotations exactly; the gate compares all three and this list is a fourth check, not a fourth source of truth.

job.role: maintenance (BYPASSRLS); the app role produces an empty archive and the script refuses it

$comment: Which mechanism covers each table, declared per table rather than inferred.
This exists because of the 'new table added later without a backup entry' edge
case, and the two ways it can be got wrong. If the gate only asked 'is this
table in scope.json', then the 40-odd Plan A tables would read as unbacked -
which is false, they are covered by the managed base backup - and whoever
maintained it would either add them to the selectable archive (wrong: the
CronJob is a deliberate subset) or delete the check. So the assignment is
explicit, every table gets a tier, and the gate requires the assignment to
be total over what the migrations create.
selectable-archive   dumped by deploy/k8s/backup-cronjob.yaml, restorable with
pg_restore and no provider CLI. The seven groups + parents.
primary-base-backup  covered by the managed PostgreSQL base backup + WAL, which
is a full-database mechanism. Selectable only via PITR, and
PITR is UNVERIFIED (gap F1/F2) - which is why the tiers are
recorded separately instead of being collapsed into 'yes'.
not-restored         deliberately excluded, with the reason. Queues redrive from
the outbox; EF history is the schema authority.

notRestored.outbox_message: MassTransit outbox. Recovery is redrive-from-outbox, never a queue restore (docs/dr/backup-restore.md, 'Schedules').
notRestored.inbox_state: MassTransit inbox deduplication state. Rederived as messages are consumed; a restored state is a dedupe window that would hide a redelivery.
notRestored.outbox_state: MassTransit transport statistics, not product state.

infrastructure.$comment: Created by EF Core, not by a migration, so the CreateTable scan cannot see it. Declared here so the gate's totality check has something to check: EF adds __EFMigrationsHistory to every database it migrates, and a restore that brought back a history disagreeing with the code would be a restore that applies the wrong migrations.
infrastructure.__EFMigrationsHistory: EF Core migration history. The migration chain is the schema authority for a restore, not an artefact one; the migration Job re-applies forward from it.

rpo.$comment: Recovery POINT objective: how much data may be lost. RPO is a property of the mechanism, not of a job's schedule. The CronJob is hourly and is explicitly NOT the RPO - see docs/backup.md.

targets.measuredBy: the staging PITR drill (docs/dr/drill-log.md), which has not run
the staging PITR drill (docs/dr/drill-log.md), which has not run

targets.mechanism: hourly pg_dump -Fc to versioned object storage
targets.measuredBy: the archive written during the 047 run of deploy/backup/dump.sh; it is an upper bound on the interval, not a measurement of WAL continuity

rto.$comment: Recovery TIME objective: how long until the core platform serves again. Quiesce-complete, as docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md step 7 defines it.
rto.measuredBy: the full-system drill in docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md section 5, against a staging instance
rto.consequence: A drill that misses the RTO is a FAILED drill. It does not become a passed drill with a note attached - docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md, 'A drill that misses RTO is a failed drill'.

restoreVerification.$comment: The steps a responder performs and the fields every drill record carries (Task 047 instruction 2). The commands are Plan A's and are NOT restated here; this is the checklist and the record shape.
restoreVerification.targetRule: Drill on staging only. A production drill requires an explicitly approved, time-boxed access window recorded BEFORE the first restore command (docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md step 0).

newEntitySteps.action: Confirm the target is staging and the access window is recorded.
Take a fresh restore of the target to a FRESH instance - never over the primary.
Count-check every scoped table, non-zero, against the expected floor.
Spot-read one row per group, by id, with the group's Plan B columns.
Verify RLS policies and append-only grants survived.
Verify the MEDIA half: an export download from the RESTORED database's id.
Measure the RTO as complete-minus-quiesce and record it even when it missed.

spotReads.why: The identity row every other subject is scoped to.
Authorization state; its absence is a 403 that reads as a broken release.
A pre-expand archive restores the table without these nine columns and the count still matches.
Key/value, not a count: two rows can sum to the right total and be the wrong rows.
Retention is a filter, not a delete; the expired row must be present and hidden.
Append-only history; a window missing from it is a gap to record, not a reason to refuse.
A restored Running row is a claim on a worker that no longer exists.

restoreVerification.recordRule: Partial success is recorded as FAILURE with the loss scope and a forward-fix. It is never recorded as a pass with a note.

escalation.$comment: Task 047 instruction 3. Plan B section 18.4 names no escalation contact, so the CONTACTS are placeholders to be replaced; the LADDER is the deliverable. It is the backup-specific slice of docs/runbooks/escalation.md and does not restate it.

triggers: a backup CronJob run failed (kubectl get jobs -n <ns> --selector app.kubernetes.io/component=backup)
the newest object-storage archive is older than 2h
mayDo: run scripts/restore-drill.sh against a disposable instance

triggers: a drill failed with a non-OK reason
a durable entity has no backup entry (deploy/backup/scope.json durableEntitiesNotYetBackedUp is non-empty)
the RPO was exceeded: the archive is older than the RPO for its scope
mayDo: open a gap in docs/backup.md with an owner
mayNotDo: promote to production with a gap open

triggers: a data-loss event, actual or suspected
a restore that cannot complete within the RTO
an archive that cannot be read by the current pg_dump
mayDo: waive a drill - as a recorded, dated decision, never as a silent one
mayNotDo: treat a recorded gap as a passed drill

escalation.drillUnavailable: A drill that cannot run because the environment is unavailable is OVERDUE, with a date and an owner. It is never waived by not running it. An overdue drill is a gap and the release gate reports it.

drills.$comment: Cadence and the record of the last run. The gate reads lastRun.date, lastRun.result and the cadence to decide DRILL_STALE / DRILL_MISSING / DRILL_FAILED. A key beginning with '$' is a comment, not a track - asserted by the gate, because a $comment read as a track produces 'this drill has no lastRun record' for a key that is not a drill.

newEntity.cadence: every release, and at least monthly
newEntity.runsOn: a disposable postgres:16-alpine started by the script; the schema comes from the committed migrations

lastRun.scope: the seven new durable-entity groups plus four parents - 10 tables, 28 synthetic rows, 7 per-group spot-reads and 15 referential checks
lastRun.resultLine: RESTORE_DRILL_RESULT reason=OK status=PASS tables=10 rows=28 gaps=0 spot=7
lastRun.target: disposable postgres:16-alpine 16.15 on 127.0.0.1:55432, schema from all 7 committed migrations
lastRun.rtoMeasured: not measured - this drill times no RTO. It is a data-half check against a single node; the RTO is measured by the full-system drill (docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md section 5).
lastRun.note: gaps=0 is the drill's own counter and it is NOT the number of open gaps. The counter is what this RUN could not close; the run reused a container the script found already up, so the media-half gap did not increment it. The register above is the record of what is open, and D1a is blocking there. Conflating the two would let a green counter stand in for a green register.

fullSystem.runsOn: a staging instance with a real access window
fullSystem.requiresEnvironment: a managed PostgreSQL with WAL archiving; NOT reachable from a developer host

gaps.$comment: The register the release gate reads. An entry with blocking=true and status=open is a FAILED release gate; that is the rule, and it is the same rule docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md states in prose. Every entry needs an owner and a reviewBy date - a gap with no owner is a complaint, and a gap with no review date is never closed.

entries.summary: The media half was not restored. The new-entity drill's scope is the new tables, so a project can restore perfectly and render an empty workspace.
entries.coveredBy: docs/runbooks/backup-restore.md section 5 (full-system drill) - which has never run; see F1
entries.note: Blocking, and it stays blocking until the full-system drill runs. Recording the limit is not the same as closing it.

entries.summary: The managed-service PITR tier is unverified: WAL archive continuity, the 7-day window and the measured RTO need a real managed instance.
entries.note: Not blocking a release because the base-backup mechanism is the provider's and is not something this repository can verify from here; blocking PROMOTION, which is what fullSystem.blocksPromotion covers.

entries.summary: The PostgreSQL client is a dependency of the drill, not of the product. A host with neither Docker nor psql cannot run it.
entries.coveredBy: CI has Docker; CLIENT_UNAVAILABLE exits 2 and reports status=FAIL, never PASS
entries.note: A SKIP-shaped absence. The gate must never accept it as a pass.

entries.summary: There was no backup job. scope.json's comment and docs/backup.md's coverage table both described deploy/k8s/backup-cronjob.yaml, which did not exist, and every coverage check passed because all three sources agreed and none of them was a job.
entries.coveredBy: deploy/k8s/backup-cronjob.yaml + deploy/backup/dump.sh + Dockerfile.backup, with the seven groups as one annotation each
entries.note: Found by looking for the file the scope file named. This is D2 and D6's defect class with the subject list removed entirely: nothing disagreed, because nothing was there to disagree.

entries.summary: The backup job's network policy was one-sided. backup-allow granted egress to PostgreSQL, but no policy granted PostgreSQL INGRESS from the backup component, so under default-deny the job could not connect - and the symptom would be a connection timeout, not a message about the policy.
entries.note: A NetworkPolicy is symmetric and each half looks locally correct, so a manifest review cannot find this. The same asymmetry still exists for the migration job and is NOT fixed here - see D9.

entries.summary: The migration Job has D8's asymmetry too: migration-allow grants it PostgreSQL egress and no policy grants PostgreSQL ingress from the migration component, so under default-deny the migration cannot connect either.
entries.note: Deliberately not fixed in this task. Widening the reach of the one workload that can DDL is a security change with its own review, and doing it inside a backup task would put an unreviewed network grant in a commit whose subject is backups. The gap is the honest record: the migration job's own comment says migration-allow 'restricts this Job's egress to PostgreSQL', which reads as complete and is not.

entries.summary: A `$comment` key in policy.json was read as a drill track by the gate, producing 'drill track "$comment" has no lastRun record' - a false positive on a documentation key.
entries.coveredBy: scripts/check-backup-policy.mjs skips $-prefixed keys, and tools/backup-policy.test.mjs asserts the gate does not report one as a track
entries.note: Found by reading the gate's output rather than its exit code: it exited 1, correctly, for two real reasons, and the third line was noise. A gate that reports noise trains people to skim it.

entries.summary: The new per-group spot-read could not distinguish the right row from the right characters: user_preferences was read on user_id alone, half of its composite key, returning three rows, and grep -q passed on the concatenation.
entries.coveredBy: scripts/restore-drill.sh takes composite predicates and asserts each read resolves to exactly one row; the failure is demonstrated by re-seeding ui.theme as "solarized" and re-running
entries.note: The D5 failure (a restore that passes on counts and fails on data) inside the check written to catch D5. Found by reading the drill's printed output: it showed three values for a read that should have shown one, and reported success.

entries.summary: Four of the seven groups were verified by count only. 043C's spot-read was a single three-table join, so preferences, activity events, memberships and voice preview jobs had no data-level assertion at all.
entries.coveredBy: one spot-read per group in scripts/restore-drill.sh (SPOT_CHECKS, with a held constant SPOT_REQUIRED=7), plus a nine-column assertion against information_schema.columns
entries.note: Invisible because the step reported success. D5 one level down, in the step whose entire purpose was to catch D5.

entries.summary: The backup job's table list was assigned to GROUPS, which bash reserves as a special array of the current user's group ids. The assignment is silently ineffective, so the job iterated the uid and dumped nothing.
entries.coveredBy: renamed to SCOPE_GROUPS/SCOPE_PARENTS in deploy/backup/dump.sh; scripts/check-backup-policy.mjs parses those exact names and treats an empty parse as a finding rather than as 'no gaps'
entries.note: Found by RUNNING the script, which is the only way to see it: `bash -n` accepts it and a reader cannot. The failure was loud (`malformed group entry: 1000`, exit 127) - a looser entry check would have dumped an empty archive and reported success. The same run found a second defect: the table-resolution loop sat above the function definitions, so the first failure died with `finish: command not found` instead of the reason that went wrong.

entries.summary: A missing PostgreSQL client in the backup image produced `psql: command not found` and exit 127 with no BACKUP_DUMP_RESULT line, so a release job parsing that line would find nothing.
entries.coveredBy: a preflight for psql, pg_dump and curl in deploy/backup/dump.sh, reporting CLIENT_UNAVAILABLE
entries.note: Found by running the script on a host without a client, which is an ordinary developer machine and not the container the job runs in. `set -e` does not help: a command-not-found inside a command substitution is reported by the shell, not by the script.

entries.summary: The S3 sink used to verify the job's signed PUT answered 200 to any request with a non-empty Authorization header, so it 'verified' an UNSIGNED upload - because curl's --user sends Basic auth when --aws-sigv4 is absent.
entries.coveredBy: the sink now requires the AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 prefix, and both the signed and the unsigned path were then run against it
entries.note: The verification harness had the same defect as every gate in this repository's history: a stub permissive enough to pass anything. Recorded because the lesson generalises - a test double that does not fail on the thing it is testing for is not a test double, it is a mirror.

entries.summary: No full-system restore drill has ever run. The drill log's three earlier entries are procedure walk-throughs and a compose sanity check; the live managed-instance tier is STAGING-GATED in every one of them.
entries.coveredBy: nothing - it needs a staging environment with an access window
entries.note: Blocking promotion, not every release. This is the entry that makes 'a drill that cannot run is overdue, not waived' mechanical: there is no date here, and an absent date is what the gate reads.

entries.summary: The RTO is a target with no measurement behind it. Nothing in this repository has timed a full restore.
entries.note: rto.measured is false in this file. A target with measured=false is honest; a target presented as a measurement is not, and the gate reports the difference.

entries.summary: The 43 primary-base-backup tables are recoverable only by PITR, and PITR is unverified. Their stated 5-minute RPO is a property of the managed service's configuration, not something observed here.
entries.note: This is why tableTiers keeps the tiers separate instead of collapsing them into 'covered': an operator reading 'backed up' for a table whose only path is an unverified PITR is misled exactly when it matters.

releaseGate.$comment: Instruction 5. Stated as data so the gate and the documentation cannot state different rules.
releaseGate.rule: An open backup/restore gap blocks the release. blocking=true with status=open fails scripts/check-backup-policy.mjs, which deploy/verify.sh runs in its static tier, so the release gate cannot pass with one open.
releaseGate.resultLine: BACKUP_GATE_RESULT reason=<REASON> status=<PASS|FAIL> groups=<n> tables=<n> gaps=<n> open=<n> blocking=<n>
wiredInto: .github/workflows/basic-ci.yml (backend job, non-blocking for a PR that only adds a table until the config is updated - the gate fails, which is the point)
releaseGate.exceptions: L3 may waive a drill, as a recorded dated decision in this file. There is no exception that makes an open gap a pass without an entry here, because the entry is the record and the gate reads the record.
